For that matter, we would also love a magic wand that would cure all disease and leave health care finance unnecessary. We might even be willing to withdraw our support for Prop 40 in exchange for such a magic wand.
But there are no magic wands, and no politically viable proposal on the table would address California’s upcoming health care woes at anything close to the same scale. The practical near-term choice for California is between using Prop 40 to offset a substantial share of the federal health care cuts and leaving them largely unoffset. Why six Nobel Prize economists back California’s Proposition 40: ‘It’s the first opportunity for the people to start reining in the power of billionaires’
Daron Acemoglu, Paul Krugman and Joseph Stiglitz, among others, signed a letter defending a one-time 5% tax on individuals whose wealth is above $1 billion. The initiative will be submitted to a vote on November 3

California is home to some of the world’s largest fortunes (https://english.elpais.com/economy-and-business/2026-05-09/the-immense-power-of-the-new-plutocracy-how-billionaires-like-musk-bezos-and-zuckerberg-shape-our-lives-and-our-democracies.html): Mark Zuckerberg, founder of Meta; Jensen Huang, chairman and co-founder of NVIDIA; and Larry Page and Sergey Brin, co-founders of Google. Together the four hold nearly $1 trillion. They top a list of about 200 billionaires who, if California’s Proposition 40 is approved at the ballot box on November 3, would be subject to a one-time 5% tax on their wealth (not their income).
This is an unprecedented initiative. And six Nobel Prize–winning economists — Daron Acemoglu, Abhijit Banerjee, Peter Diamond, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman and Joseph Stiglitz — say the model should be extended worldwide in response to what they describe as an unequal tax contribution by the wealthiest families (https://english.elpais.com/usa/2026-08-18/a-government-of-multimillionaires-trump-appointed-57-officials-worth-as-much-as-100-million.html).
“If the state that houses some of the country’s most powerful billionaires votes to tax their wealth, it will kickstart a movement to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals in other states — and eventually at the federal level and in other countries,” the letter says. “As Californians head to the polls, their vote may well come to be seen as a turning point in the battle between democracy and oligarchy.”
In California alone, the 200 ultra-rich individuals who would be subject to the levy hold an estimated $2.3 trillion in wealth — roughly equal to the state’s annual gross domestic product of a state that is home to 39 million people. Their mansions are in Beverly Hills, Los Angeles, Newport Beach and Silicon Valley (https://english.elpais.com/opinion/2026-03-15/the-new-robber-barons-are-the-tech-tycoons.html). They represent just 0.001% of the population and, between 2023 and 2025, the wealth of several of them rose by 144% driven by the boom in artificial intelligence, according to a study by the National Bureau of Economic Research. Other large fortunes that could also be affected by the tax include those of Dario Amodei, co-founder of Anthropic; Travis Kalanick, co-founder of Uber; Peter Thiel, co-founder of PayPal; and Jan Koum, co-founder of WhatsApp.
Mark Zuckerberg, in California, September 25, 2024. Godofredo A. Vásquez (AP Photo/Godofredo A. Vásquez) Fewer taxes, but more power
Proposition 40 would require California residents with wealth above $1 billion to pay a one-time tax equal to 5% of the total value of their assets. Its backer, the Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), estimates the measure would raise about $100 billion. Ninety percent of those funds would finance health care, which the group says was harmed by cuts under the Donald Trump administration, while the remaining 10% would be split between food assistance and education programs.
If voters approve it on November 3 with more than 50% of the vote, the tax would apply to people who have been California residents since January 1 of this year. In other words, those who leave the state after the election could not avoid the levy.
“Over the 2019-2025 period, the total amount of California income tax paid by billionaires amounted to only 1.6% of their $1.4 trillion wealth gain, much less than what ordinary Californians pay on their paychecks,” the letter notes.
The economists also question how those fortunes were built and the political power these figures have amassed through contributions to political campaigns: “How did the billionaires get to be so rich (https://english.elpais.com/economy-and-business/2026-01-17/a-year-of-movement-among-worlds-20-richest-with-elon-musk-almost-untouchable-at-the-top.html)? In many cases, they made important contributions, for which they have been amply rewarded. But our failure to tax their returns on capital—a myriad of loopholes they’ve taken full advantage of—has also allowed their wealth to compound, while ordinary Americans have paid higher rates.”
Sergey Brin’s campaign
Four people — Mark Zuckerberg, Jensen Huang, Larry Page and Sergey Brin — alone own about 40% of all wealth held by California’s billionaires. While Huang, NVIDIA’s chief executive, has said he is willing to give up 5% of his fortune, Brin, one of Google’s early backers, is leading a $100 million ad campaign to defeat Proposition 40 at the ballot box.
Sergey Brin, at Stanford, California. Jeff Chiu (AP) His argument is that the tax scheme is poorly designed and could drive some billionaires to other states, resulting in lost tax revenue, jobs and investments. “When the money runs out, Sacramento will come back with another tax,” warns one of the ads paid for by the committee Building a Better California .
Brin, whose family left the Soviet Union when he was a child, says the fight has become personal. “I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and I know the oppressive and devastating society that system created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same situation,” he told the New York Times .
Those who drafted Proposition 40 dismiss Brin’s arguments. The SEIU-UHW says his wealth has doubled to nearly $300 billion since Donald Trump’s election, and notes that Brin was one of his donors. The union says he is part of a “small group of billionaires” who, it claims, spread falsehoods about the measure in order to avoid paying the tax.
Opposition is organized in several committees, including the California Business Roundtable, which presents the measure as a “tax on everyone.” Also opposing it are the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Teachers Association and the California Association of Children’s Hospitals.
The initiative has also opened a rift within the Democratic Party. Progressive Senator Bernie Sanders backs it. “The idea that they say it’s OK for kids to die, that people won’t get the health care they need, that they’re going to punish Californians... is outrageous,” he said. The state party leadership also supports it.
At the other end is Governor Gavin Newsom, who has presidential ambitions, and who questions the structure of the measure and says a tax of this kind should be applied nationally. He warns about the potential relocation of billionaires and their investments out of California. “This poorly designed state measure will take resources away from teachers, schools, clinics and public safety,” he said in a statement quoted by the Los Angeles Times .
Support hangs in the balance
The future of Proposition 40 is uncertain. Polls show a narrow edge for the “Yes” vote, although support drops among voters who say they are more familiar with the initiative.
Joseph Stiglitz, in Madrid. Alvaro Garcia The Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) found in a poll published this week that 52% of voters support the measure, while 46% oppose it. A month earlier, a survey by the Institute of Governmental Studies (IGS) at the University of California, Berkeley recorded 48% support and 41% opposition.
Another poll, conducted by Politico and UC Berkeley’s Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research, put support this week at 45%, with 43% opposed and 12% undecided. However, among respondents who said they had heard “a lot” about the proposal, opposition reached 57% versus 38% in favor.
In 2022 Californians rejected Proposition 30, an initiative that would have raised taxes on higher earners. The result was 58% against and 42% in favor. The measure proposed raising the income tax by 1.75 percentage points on those earning more than $2 million a year and directing the new revenue to zero-emission vehicle programs and fire prevention.
In that context, the six Nobel Prize economists argue that, while Proposition 40 would not by itself solve the problem of inequality in California, it would represent a step in the right direction. “What will allow California to thrive in the future is not letting a handful of billionaires live tax free: it is adequate public spending on health, education, and public infrastructure, key engines of economic growth to which it is only fair to ask the ultra-wealthy to contribute,” they write.

California is home to some of the world’s largest fortunes (https://english.elpais.com/economy-and-business/2026-05-09/the-immense-power-of-the-new-plutocracy-how-billionaires-like-musk-bezos-and-zuckerberg-shape-our-lives-and-our-democracies.html): Mark Zuckerberg, founder of Meta; Jensen Huang, chairman and co-founder of NVIDIA; and Larry Page and Sergey Brin, co-founders of Google. Together the four hold nearly $1 trillion. They top a list of about 200 billionaires who, if California’s Proposition 40 is approved at the ballot box on November 3, would be subject to a one-time 5% tax on their wealth (not their income).
This is an unprecedented initiative. And six Nobel Prize–winning economists — Daron Acemoglu, Abhijit Banerjee, Peter Diamond, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman and Joseph Stiglitz — say the model should be extended worldwide in response to what they describe as an unequal tax contribution by the wealthiest families (https://english.elpais.com/usa/2026-08-18/a-government-of-multimillionaires-trump-appointed-57-officials-worth-as-much-as-100-million.html).
“If the state that houses some of the country’s most powerful billionaires votes to tax their wealth, it will kickstart a movement to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals in other states — and eventually at the federal level and in other countries,” the letter says. “As Californians head to the polls, their vote may well come to be seen as a turning point in the battle between democracy and oligarchy.”
In California alone, the 200 ultra-rich individuals who would be subject to the levy hold an estimated $2.3 trillion in wealth — roughly equal to the state’s annual gross domestic product of a state that is home to 39 million people. Their mansions are in Beverly Hills, Los Angeles, Newport Beach and Silicon Valley (https://english.elpais.com/opinion/2026-03-15/the-new-robber-barons-are-the-tech-tycoons.html). They represent just 0.001% of the population and, between 2023 and 2025, the wealth of several of them rose by 144% driven by the boom in artificial intelligence, according to a study by the National Bureau of Economic Research. Other large fortunes that could also be affected by the tax include those of Dario Amodei, co-founder of Anthropic; Travis Kalanick, co-founder of Uber; Peter Thiel, co-founder of PayPal; and Jan Koum, co-founder of WhatsApp.
Mark Zuckerberg, in California, September 25, 2024. Godofredo A. Vásquez (AP Photo/Godofredo A. Vásquez) Fewer taxes, but more power
Proposition 40 would require California residents with wealth above $1 billion to pay a one-time tax equal to 5% of the total value of their assets. Its backer, the Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), estimates the measure would raise about $100 billion. Ninety percent of those funds would finance health care, which the group says was harmed by cuts under the Donald Trump administration, while the remaining 10% would be split between food assistance and education programs.
If voters approve it on November 3 with more than 50% of the vote, the tax would apply to people who have been California residents since January 1 of this year. In other words, those who leave the state after the election could not avoid the levy.
“Over the 2019-2025 period, the total amount of California income tax paid by billionaires amounted to only 1.6% of their $1.4 trillion wealth gain, much less than what ordinary Californians pay on their paychecks,” the letter notes.
The economists also question how those fortunes were built and the political power these figures have amassed through contributions to political campaigns: “How did the billionaires get to be so rich (https://english.elpais.com/economy-and-business/2026-01-17/a-year-of-movement-among-worlds-20-richest-with-elon-musk-almost-untouchable-at-the-top.html)? In many cases, they made important contributions, for which they have been amply rewarded. But our failure to tax their returns on capital—a myriad of loopholes they’ve taken full advantage of—has also allowed their wealth to compound, while ordinary Americans have paid higher rates.”
Sergey Brin’s campaign
Four people — Mark Zuckerberg, Jensen Huang, Larry Page and Sergey Brin — alone own about 40% of all wealth held by California’s billionaires. While Huang, NVIDIA’s chief executive, has said he is willing to give up 5% of his fortune, Brin, one of Google’s early backers, is leading a $100 million ad campaign to defeat Proposition 40 at the ballot box.
Sergey Brin, at Stanford, California. Jeff Chiu (AP) His argument is that the tax scheme is poorly designed and could drive some billionaires to other states, resulting in lost tax revenue, jobs and investments. “When the money runs out, Sacramento will come back with another tax,” warns one of the ads paid for by the committee Building a Better California .
Brin, whose family left the Soviet Union when he was a child, says the fight has become personal. “I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and I know the oppressive and devastating society that system created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same situation,” he told the New York Times .
Those who drafted Proposition 40 dismiss Brin’s arguments. The SEIU-UHW says his wealth has doubled to nearly $300 billion since Donald Trump’s election, and notes that Brin was one of his donors. The union says he is part of a “small group of billionaires” who, it claims, spread falsehoods about the measure in order to avoid paying the tax.
Opposition is organized in several committees, including the California Business Roundtable, which presents the measure as a “tax on everyone.” Also opposing it are the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Teachers Association and the California Association of Children’s Hospitals.
The initiative has also opened a rift within the Democratic Party. Progressive Senator Bernie Sanders backs it. “The idea that they say it’s OK for kids to die, that people won’t get the health care they need, that they’re going to punish Californians... is outrageous,” he said. The state party leadership also supports it.
At the other end is Governor Gavin Newsom, who has presidential ambitions, and who questions the structure of the measure and says a tax of this kind should be applied nationally. He warns about the potential relocation of billionaires and their investments out of California. “This poorly designed state measure will take resources away from teachers, schools, clinics and public safety,” he said in a statement quoted by the Los Angeles Times .
Support hangs in the balance
The future of Proposition 40 is uncertain. Polls show a narrow edge for the “Yes” vote, although support drops among voters who say they are more familiar with the initiative.
Joseph Stiglitz, in Madrid. Alvaro Garcia The Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) found in a poll published this week that 52% of voters support the measure, while 46% oppose it. A month earlier, a survey by the Institute of Governmental Studies (IGS) at the University of California, Berkeley recorded 48% support and 41% opposition.
Another poll, conducted by Politico and UC Berkeley’s Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research, put support this week at 45%, with 43% opposed and 12% undecided. However, among respondents who said they had heard “a lot” about the proposal, opposition reached 57% versus 38% in favor.
In 2022 Californians rejected Proposition 30, an initiative that would have raised taxes on higher earners. The result was 58% against and 42% in favor. The measure proposed raising the income tax by 1.75 percentage points on those earning more than $2 million a year and directing the new revenue to zero-emission vehicle programs and fire prevention.
In that context, the six Nobel Prize economists argue that, while Proposition 40 would not by itself solve the problem of inequality in California, it would represent a step in the right direction. “What will allow California to thrive in the future is not letting a handful of billionaires live tax free: it is adequate public spending on health, education, and public infrastructure, key engines of economic growth to which it is only fair to ask the ultra-wealthy to contribute,” they write.

Economists (71%) and Accountants (85%) Oppose California’s Billionaire Tax; 60% of Tax Lawyers Support It
Paul Caron (https://taxprofblog.aals.org/author/pcaron/)
October 18, 2026
Uncategorized (https://taxprofblog.aals.org/category/uncategorized/)
Jeffrey L. Hoopes (North Carolina), What Do Tax Experts Think About California’s Billionaire Tax? (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7612139):
This brief note reports the results of a survey of tax experts regarding California’s Proposition 40, a proposed one-time tax on billionaire wealth. Among 105 respondents, 69.5 percent opposed the proposal, including 71.0 percent of economists and 85.0 percent of accountants. Lawyers were more supportive, with 60.0 percent favoring the tax. Open-ended responses reveal concerns about taxpayer mobility, revenue losses, valuation difficulties, and administrative costs. The results contrast with the public endorsement of the proposal by six Nobel Prize-winning economists and highlight differences in opinion among scholars who specialize in taxation. Opinions about Prop 40 embed knowledge of the relevant empirical literature, interpretation of the empirical literature, and the values of the person holding the opinion, such that differences between groups in opinion might reflect any of these factors.
Conclusion
Six Nobel Prize-winning economists have endorsed Proposition 40. Among the respondents to this survey, however, economists and accountants who study taxes in their everyday work overwhelmingly oppose it, while lawyers are divided, marginally supporting it. Overall, surveyed tax experts would not vote for Prop 40.
Some of the relevant questions for assessing this piece of legislation are empirical. How many wealthy individuals will leave California? How much revenue will the tax actually raise? These are questions on which academic research can shed light. But whether the tax is desirable also depends on values, including how big government should be, who should pay for it, and how many economic resources we are willing to use up in the process of collecting revenue. Academic tax experts have expertise that can help answer the empirical questions, but their values are no more important than anyone else’s, even if they have likely thought about these tax issues more. However, in the end, considering both the empirical evidence they are aware of and their values, the tax scholars responding to this survey do not support Proposition 40 by a substantial margin.

choices of wealthy individuals by examining the geographical sensitiv-
ity of the Forbes 400 richest Americans to state estate taxes. Though
we find billionaires’ effective tax rates are only about half the statutory
rate, their residential choices are highly sensitive to these taxes, as 35
percent of local billionaires leave states with an estate tax. This tax-in-
duced mobility causes a large reduction in the aggregate tax base.
Nonetheless, we find that the revenue benefit of an estate tax exceeds
the cost for the vast majority of states. (JEL H24, H31, H71, R23)
The United States exhibits vast geographical differences in the degree to which
personal income, corporate income, and wealth are taxed. There has been much
debate in recent years on the costs and benefits of state and local governments
imposing high taxes on their richest residents and most profitable firms, especially
in light of the potential for tax flight (Moretti and Wilson 2017; Kleven et al. 2020;
Slattery and Zidar 2020). But despite the strong interest of policymakers and voters,
the effect of state and local taxes on the geographical location of wealthy individuals
and businesses is not fully understood. Although there have been some important
recent advances, there is still too little empirical work on the effect of taxation on the
spatial mobility of individuals, especially among high-income individuals.
In this paper, we contribute to the literature on the effect of state taxes on the
locational choices of wealthy individuals by studying how estate taxes affect the
state of residence of the American ultra-rich and the implications for tax policy.
The estate tax (ET) is essentially a wealth tax imposed on the very wealthy at the
time of death (Kopczuk 2009). Specifically, we estimate the effects of state-level
estate taxes on the geographical location of the Forbes 400 richest Americans

We find that billionaires’ geographical location is highly sensitive to state estate
taxes. Billionaires tend to leave states with an estate tax, especially as they get old.
But despite the high tax mobility, we find that the revenue benefit of an estate tax
exceeds the cost for the vast majority of states.
Estate taxes on the ultra-wealthy have potentially important consequences both
for taxpayer families and for state governments. Given the rise of wealth owned by
those at the top of the distribution, taxes on large estates have a growing potential to
significantly impact states’ entire budgets. Consider, for example, David Koch, who
died in August 2019 with an estimated net worth of $50.5 billion. He was a resident
of New York state, which has an estate tax. Given our estimate of the effective state
estate tax rate (which accounts for typical charitable deductions and sheltering),
New York should eventually expect to receive revenues of around $4.17 billion.1 For
the richest of the Forbes 400, the effect is even larger. As of the time of this writing,
Jeff Bezos is the richest person in the United States, with an estimated net worth of
roughly $200 billion according to Forbes. He resides in Washington state, which
has an estate tax. If he died today, his estate could expect to incur a state tax bill of
around $21 billion, almost doubling Washington state’s total tax revenues from all
sources in a single year. Of course, the typical impact of a Forbes 400 death on state
revenues is smaller, though far from trivial, given that the median person in the 2017
Forbes 400 has estimated net worth of “only” $3.7 billion.
We begin the empirical analysis by investigating the quality of the Forbes 400
data. While prior research has found that individual net worth reported by Forbes is
consistent with IRS confidential tax return data (Saez and Zucman 2016), there has
been no previous assessment of Forbes data on state of residence. We conduct an
audit using published obituaries of deceased Forbes 400 individuals. State of death
is likely to be highly correlated with the true state of residence, as people are more
likely to die in their true primary residence state than in any other state.2 We find
that the state of residence listed by Forbes matches the state listed in obituaries in
90 percent of cases.
Furthermore, for each billionaire death, we estimate the effect on estate tax rev-
enues of the state that Forbes identifies as the one of residence. We find a sharp and
economically large increase in estate tax revenues in the three years after a Forbes
billionaire’s death. We estimate that, on average, a Forbes billionaire’s death results
in an increase in state estate revenues of $165 million. Our estimate implies an
effective tax rate of 8.25 percent after allowing for charitable and spousal deduc-
tions, and tax avoidance—a rate that is a little over half of the statutory rate. This
rate is consistent with IRS estimates of federal estate tax liability for this group of
taxpayers.
Having validated the Forbes data, we turn to the core of our empirical analysis,
namely the sensitivity of the ultra-wealthy’s locational choice to estate taxes. We

We first use a double-difference estimator to estimate the differential effect of
having an estate tax before versus after 2001 on the number of Forbes 400 indi-
viduals in a state. We find that before 2001, there is a slight positive correlation

average, estate tax states lose 2.35 Forbes 400 individuals relative to non–estate tax

that the OLS result is not due to endogenous estate tax adoption or repeal after the
2001 reform.
We then turn to a triple-difference estimator based on the notion that a billion-
aire’s sensitivity to the estate tax should increase as they age. In terms of identifica-

changes in estate tax status after 2001. We find that the number of older Forbes

Forbes billionaires. The elasticity of location with respect to estate taxes for older
billionaires is significantly higher than the elasticity for the younger billionaires.3
As an alternative way to quantify the effect of estate taxes on Forbes billion-
aires’ locational choices, we study the probability that individuals who are observed
residing in estate tax states before the reform move to non–estate tax states after
the reform, and, inversely, the probability that individuals who are observed living
in non–estate tax states before the reform move to an estate tax states afterward.
Among billionaires observed in 2001, we find a high probability of moving from
estate tax states to non–estate tax states after 2001 and a low probability of moving
from non–estate tax states to estate tax states. By year 2010—namely, 9 years after
the reform—21.4 percent of individuals who originally were in an estate tax state
had moved to a non–estate tax state, while only 1.2 percent of individuals who orig-
inally were in a non–estate tax state had moved to an estate tax state. The difference
is significantly more pronounced for individuals 65 or older, consistent with the
triple-difference models.

to state estate taxes. The 2001 federal tax reform introduced large differences in

Surprisingly, despite the high tax mobility elasticity, we find that for most states the
benefit of additional revenues from adopting an estate tax significantly exceeds the
cost of forgone income tax revenue due to tax-induced mobility.
The cost-benefit ratio is 0.69 for the average state, indicating that the additional
revenues from an estate tax exceed the loss of revenues from forgone income taxes
by 31 percent. The ratio varies across states as a function of the state income tax
rate and, to a lesser extent, the ages of the state’s billionaires. In California, the
cost-benefit ratio is 1.45, indicating that if California adopted the estate tax on
billionaires, the state would lose revenues by a significant margin. (Currently,
California does not have an estate tax.) The high cost reflects the very high top tax

the state has a high opportunity cost in terms of forgone personal income tax rev-

no income tax. The adoption of an estate tax in these states increases tax revenues
unambiguously. We estimate that state revenues in Florida and Texas would increase
by $7.67 billion and $7.06 billion, respectively, if the states adopted an estate tax.
Overall, we estimate that 28 of the 29 states that currently do not have an estate tax
and have at least 1 billionaire would experience revenue gains if they adopted an
estate tax on billionaires, with California the lone exception.

Finally, we extend the analysis to consider the costs and benefits of adopting a
broader estate tax, one that applies not only to billionaires but to all taxpayers with
estate values above $5.5 million for individuals and $11 million for couples (the
current federal thresholds). We find that the policy implications for states that we
draw based on a billionaire estate tax generally extend to a broad estate tax: for most
states, the benefits of adopting an estate tax exceed the costs, whether the tax is
imposed on the ultra-wealthy or the merely wealthy.
Our paper seeks to advance the literature on the sensitivity of high-income indi-
viduals’ locational choices to state and local taxes. We focus on wealth, while most
of the previous literature has focused on personal income taxes. For example, Moretti
and Wilson (2017) and Akcigit, Baslandze, and Stantcheva (2016) find evidence
that top patenters, who have very high income, are quite sensitive to income taxes
in their choice of location. Rauh and Shyu (2019) find similar results for high-in-
come taxpayers in California. On the other hand, Young et al. (2016) and Young and
Varner (2011) find limited evidence of tax-induced mobility of millionaires. Kleven
et al. (2020) have a recent survey of the literature.6 Overall, despite the importance
of the question for state and local governments, the exact magnitude of the elastic-
ities of the number of rich taxpayers with respect to specific forms of subnational
taxation is still poorly documented. As a consequence, much of the policy debate
and actual tax policy choices are based on policymaker ideological priors rather than
solid empirical facts.
The literature on the geographic sensitivity of individuals to estate taxes is even

I. Background and Key Facts on State Estate Taxes
A. History and Structure
State-level estate taxes in the United States date back to the early nineteenth
century, predating the 1916 adoption of the federal estate tax. In 1924, a federal
estate tax credit was enacted for state estate tax payments, up to a limit. This credit
remained in place for the rest of the twentieth century.9 The credit rate schedule pre-
vailing from 1954 to 2001 is shown in online Appendix Table B1 (based on table 1
of Bakija and Slemrod 2004). The top marginal credit rate of 16 percent applied to
all estate values above $10,040,000. Thus, for estates far above this value—such as
those of the Forbes 400—both the marginal and average credit rate was 16 percent.

TaxProf Blog Op-Ed: Galle et al. on “Tax Reform, Health Care Finance, and the Case for Prop 40”
Jon Endean (https://taxprofblog.aals.org/author/jendean/)
October 21, 2026
Tax (https://taxprofblog.aals.org/category/tax/) , Tax Profs (https://taxprofblog.aals.org/category/tax-profs/) , Tax Scholarship (https://taxprofblog.aals.org/category/tax-scholarship/)
This TaxProf Op-Ed on California’s Proposition 40 is by Brian Galle (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/our-faculty/faculty-profiles/brian-galle/#tab_profile) (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (https://law.missouri.edu/directory/david-gamage/) (Missouri), and Darien Shanske (https://law.ucdavis.edu/people/darien-shanske) (UC Davis):
Tax Reform, Health Care Finance, and the Case for Prop 40: California’s Billionaire Wealth Tax
Brian Galle, David Gamage, and Darien Shanske 1
Chocolate and peanut butter; tax reform and health care finance. In California’s upcoming November election, these are two great tastes that go well together.
We know that many TaxProf Blog readers have heard about the billionaire tax. We thought it would be worthwhile to introduce the issues ourselves. California’s Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires who were California residents as of January 1, 2026, payable over five years with an interest deferral charge, so roughly equivalent to a 1% annual wealth tax but assessed for only five years. Ninety percent of the revenue is dedicated to health care, the rest to education and food assistance. 2 Without Prop 40, California must absorb federal cuts that RAND estimates will reduce funding for its Medicaid program by roughly $112 billion through 2034, an amount equivalent to more than $8,000 per California household. 3 To help offset that cut, essentially a stupendously regressive tax meant to (partially!) finance stupendously regressive tax cuts, we helped draft and design Prop 40, and write here to refute some claims by opponents. 4
Tax Reform: Revenue, Mobility and Avoidance
Professor Emmanuel Saez, who worked to design Prop 40 with us, estimated that the tax could raise about $100 billion or about $20 billion per year for five years. 5 An analysis by Blue Sky Consulting Group agrees and estimates that Prop 40 will raise $116 billion in revenues, approximately $23 billion a year for five years. 6 Even modeling Prop 40 as if it were a permanent 1 percent annual tax, for purposes of generating a high-end estimate of mobility and tax avoidance, Blue Sky’s upper-bound estimate of lost income and sales tax from future departures is only $640 million a year – less than 3 percent of the annual wealth tax revenues raised.
The effects of Prop 40 on income tax revenues are tiny because, among other reasons, the existing income tax at both the federal and state levels mostly fails to meaningfully reach billionaires. Scholarship by Gamage and Brooks estimates that most ultra-wealthy taxpayers realize less than a quarter of their true investment income as taxable income over their lifetime, so over three-quarters is never subject to personal income tax. 7 Economists similarly estimate that California’s billionaires pay only about 0.2 percent of their wealth each year in California income tax. 8 Meanwhile, the ordinary rich who earn salary income face the highest state income tax rates in the country.
There is thus a strong case for using a wealth tax to supplement and fill the gaps in the income tax. 9 We offered a more comprehensive case for state-level wealth taxes in prior scholarship, including assessing misplaced concerns about mobility. 10 Moreover, for those who favor federal-level reform, history implies that a successful state-level wealth tax reform will likely be needed first, just as early state income taxes, most notably Wisconsin’s in 1911, helped pave the way for the modern federal income tax enacted in 1913. 11
California’s billionaires pay relatively little income tax, and yet they have benefitted extraordinarily from California’s booming economy and productive workforce. Indeed, despite all the attention paid to billionaire departures, among those who were California residents on January 1, 2026, and so potentially subject to Prop 40, the number of billionaires has grown from 240 to 260 this year, and their combined wealth has grown from about $2.05 trillion to about $2.44 trillion. 12 A one-time 5 percent tax would thus take less than a third of just this year’s increase in that group’s wealth, for use in keeping health care available for all Californians.
Health Care Finance: The OBBBA’s Cuts and the Magic Wand Response
Last year’s federal budget law, the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), paid for part of its tax cuts by slashing federal health care spending by about $1.1 trillion over ten years. CBO estimates roughly $990 billion of reductions in Medicaid and CHIP and another $213 billion from changes to ACA marketplace subsidies, partly offset by increased spending elsewhere. 13 In California, the state’s Medicaid/Medi-Cal agency estimates that up to 2 million enrollees could lose coverage and that tens of billions of federal dollars are at risk each year. 14 These cuts will mostly begin impacting California in 2027, with new work-reporting requirements starting in January and six-month eligibility checks in March. The Legislative Analyst’s Office projects that the number of uninsured Californians could double by 2030. 15
Medicaid/Medi-Cal does a great deal of good. Research finds that the ACA’s Medicaid expansion reduced deaths among beneficiaries. 16 An Oregon study found that coverage nearly eliminated catastrophic out-of-pocket spending. 17 Children covered by Medicaid eventually earn more and pay more tax, so the program recoups much of its costs. 18 Medicaid helps keep hospitals open, especially rural hospitals. 19 Medicaid also benefits hospitals and clinics by paying for care they would otherwise provide without compensation. 20
Some critics claim Prop 40 is the wrong approach for health care finance. For instance, Katie Porter has called it a measure that “just perpetuates the status quo.” 21
We would welcome comprehensive health reform, 22 but this is not easy to accomplish, especially at the state level. For instance, California’s single-payer bills have repeatedly died in the Legislature, most recently this year when AB 1900 was shelved without a hearing, and have no prospects of passing anytime soon. 23 We are unwilling to see families lose coverage or absorb these cuts in order to facilitate a transition to a new health insurance system, especially one that seems unlikely to arrive any time soon.
We would love to find a magic wand that could accomplish comprehensive health reform. For that matter, we would also love a magic wand that would cure all disease and leave health care finance unnecessary. We might even be willing to withdraw our support for Prop 40 in exchange for such a magic wand.
But there are no magic wands, and no politically viable proposal on the table would address California’s upcoming health care woes at anything close to the same scale. The practical near-term choice for California is between using Prop 40 to offset a substantial share of the federal health care cuts and leaving them largely unoffset. Opponents of Prop 40 offer no comparably scaled alternative that could arrive in time, only magical thinking.
Why One-Time?
We have argued that tax reform (e.g., billionaire wealth taxes) and health care finance (e.g., preserving Medicaid/Medi-Cal) go together synergistically, as two great tastes – but there is a tension.
In the past, we have drafted and supported proposals for an ongoing annual 1% wealth tax for California that would have applied to roughly 15,000 of the state’s wealthiest families. 24 As we developed that earlier work, we were told that California’s tax agencies would request years to set up the computer systems and information reporting needed to make an ongoing annual tax on a new base (wealth) work. 25 By contrast, a one-time tax can operate more like the federal estate tax, with wealth valued and reported once rather than every year. If it passes, Prop 40 will value each billionaire’s wealth once, as of December 31, 2026. With only about 250 taxpayers, Prop 40 is designed so that FTB can begin collecting revenue in 2027, along with the income tax filing deadline. 26
With the OBBBA’s cuts to health care in California expected to have major harmful impact beginning in 2027, a tax solution is needed that can raise sufficient revenues in 2027. Thus, at least for now, Prop 40’s one-time approach is what California needs.
Five years of revenue raising, starting in 2027, will bolster California’s health care finances well into a new presidential administration and Congress. This buys time to see whether the federal government restores health care funding or whether we might get comprehensive health care reform at either the federal or state level.
The Poison Pills of Props 41 and 42
Prop 40 is threatened by two other ballot measures, Propositions 41 and 42, both backed by a committee funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin, and designed as poison pills intended to undermine Prop 40. 27 As we explain elsewhere, the deceptive language of Props 41 and 42 could threaten much more than just Prop 40—including threats to the health plan and hospital taxes that currently help fund Medi-Cal. 28 Supporters of Prop 40 must vote against Props 41 and 42, because both include hidden provisions that could keep Prop 40 from taking effect if either gets more “yes” votes than Prop 40. Indeed, even principled opponents of Prop 40 should vote against Props 41 and 42 because they undermine democracy and likely would have unfortunate unforeseen consequences.
Media and Democracy
Finally, consider the motivations of many of the critics of Prop 40; for instance, the LA Times editorial against it. 29 According to former LA Times editorials editor Mariel Garza, the paper has had no editorial writers or functioning editorial board since early 2025, after its billionaire owner chased them away. Garza does not know who wrote the editorial against Prop 40, and unlike other California papers that have met with both proponents and opponents of ballot measures to assess the arguments, the LA Times had no communications with Prop 40 proponents. As Garza notes, the billionaires who would pay Prop 40’s tax if it passes include the paper’s owner. 30 Prop 40 will not by itself come close to restoring a properly functioning American democracy. But it does offer a potential model for future legislation that might accomplish that goal.

Why six Nobel Prize economists back California’s Proposition 40: ‘It’s the first opportunity for the people to start reining in the power of billionaires’
Daron Acemoglu, Paul Krugman and Joseph Stiglitz, among others, signed a letter defending a one-time 5% tax on individuals whose wealth is above $1 billion. The initiative will be submitted to a vote on November 3

California is home to some of the world’s largest fortunes (https://english.elpais.com/economy-and-business/2026-05-09/the-immense-power-of-the-new-plutocracy-how-billionaires-like-musk-bezos-and-zuckerberg-shape-our-lives-and-our-democracies.html): Mark Zuckerberg, founder of Meta; Jensen Huang, chairman and co-founder of NVIDIA; and Larry Page and Sergey Brin, co-founders of Google. Together the four hold nearly $1 trillion. They top a list of about 200 billionaires who, if California’s Proposition 40 is approved at the ballot box on November 3, would be subject to a one-time 5% tax on their wealth (not their income).
This is an unprecedented initiative. And six Nobel Prize–winning economists — Daron Acemoglu, Abhijit Banerjee, Peter Diamond, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman and Joseph Stiglitz — say the model should be extended worldwide in response to what they describe as an unequal tax contribution by the wealthiest families (https://english.elpais.com/usa/2026-08-18/a-government-of-multimillionaires-trump-appointed-57-officials-worth-as-much-as-100-million.html).
“If the state that houses some of the country’s most powerful billionaires votes to tax their wealth, it will kickstart a movement to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals in other states — and eventually at the federal level and in other countries,” the letter says. “As Californians head to the polls, their vote may well come to be seen as a turning point in the battle between democracy and oligarchy.”
In California alone, the 200 ultra-rich individuals who would be subject to the levy hold an estimated $2.3 trillion in wealth — roughly equal to the state’s annual gross domestic product of a state that is home to 39 million people. Their mansions are in Beverly Hills, Los Angeles, Newport Beach and Silicon Valley (https://english.elpais.com/opinion/2026-03-15/the-new-robber-barons-are-the-tech-tycoons.html). They represent just 0.001% of the population and, between 2023 and 2025, the wealth of several of them rose by 144% driven by the boom in artificial intelligence, according to a study by the National Bureau of Economic Research. Other large fortunes that could also be affected by the tax include those of Dario Amodei, co-founder of Anthropic; Travis Kalanick, co-founder of Uber; Peter Thiel, co-founder of PayPal; and Jan Koum, co-founder of WhatsApp.
Mark Zuckerberg, in California, September 25, 2024. Godofredo A. Vásquez (AP Photo/Godofredo A. Vásquez) Fewer taxes, but more power
Proposition 40 would require California residents with wealth above $1 billion to pay a one-time tax equal to 5% of the total value of their assets. Its backer, the Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), estimates the measure would raise about $100 billion. Ninety percent of those funds would finance health care, which the group says was harmed by cuts under the Donald Trump administration, while the remaining 10% would be split between food assistance and education programs.
If voters approve it on November 3 with more than 50% of the vote, the tax would apply to people who have been California residents since January 1 of this year. In other words, those who leave the state after the election could not avoid the levy.
“Over the 2019-2025 period, the total amount of California income tax paid by billionaires amounted to only 1.6% of their $1.4 trillion wealth gain, much less than what ordinary Californians pay on their paychecks,” the letter notes.
The economists also question how those fortunes were built and the political power these figures have amassed through contributions to political campaigns: “How did the billionaires get to be so rich (https://english.elpais.com/economy-and-business/2026-01-17/a-year-of-movement-among-worlds-20-richest-with-elon-musk-almost-untouchable-at-the-top.html)? In many cases, they made important contributions, for which they have been amply rewarded. But our failure to tax their returns on capital—a myriad of loopholes they’ve taken full advantage of—has also allowed their wealth to compound, while ordinary Americans have paid higher rates.”
Sergey Brin’s campaign
Four people — Mark Zuckerberg, Jensen Huang, Larry Page and Sergey Brin — alone own about 40% of all wealth held by California’s billionaires. While Huang, NVIDIA’s chief executive, has said he is willing to give up 5% of his fortune, Brin, one of Google’s early backers, is leading a $100 million ad campaign to defeat Proposition 40 at the ballot box.
Sergey Brin, at Stanford, California. Jeff Chiu (AP) His argument is that the tax scheme is poorly designed and could drive some billionaires to other states, resulting in lost tax revenue, jobs and investments. “When the money runs out, Sacramento will come back with another tax,” warns one of the ads paid for by the committee Building a Better California .
Brin, whose family left the Soviet Union when he was a child, says the fight has become personal. “I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and I know the oppressive and devastating society that system created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same situation,” he told the New York Times .
Those who drafted Proposition 40 dismiss Brin’s arguments. The SEIU-UHW says his wealth has doubled to nearly $300 billion since Donald Trump’s election, and notes that Brin was one of his donors. The union says he is part of a “small group of billionaires” who, it claims, spread falsehoods about the measure in order to avoid paying the tax.
Opposition is organized in several committees, including the California Business Roundtable, which presents the measure as a “tax on everyone.” Also opposing it are the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Teachers Association and the California Association of Children’s Hospitals.
The initiative has also opened a rift within the Democratic Party. Progressive Senator Bernie Sanders backs it. “The idea that they say it’s OK for kids to die, that people won’t get the health care they need, that they’re going to punish Californians... is outrageous,” he said. The state party leadership also supports it.
At the other end is Governor Gavin Newsom, who has presidential ambitions, and who questions the structure of the measure and says a tax of this kind should be applied nationally. He warns about the potential relocation of billionaires and their investments out of California. “This poorly designed state measure will take resources away from teachers, schools, clinics and public safety,” he said in a statement quoted by the Los Angeles Times .
Support hangs in the balance
The future of Proposition 40 is uncertain. Polls show a narrow edge for the “Yes” vote, although support drops among voters who say they are more familiar with the initiative.
Joseph Stiglitz, in Madrid. Alvaro Garcia The Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) found in a poll published this week that 52% of voters support the measure, while 46% oppose it. A month earlier, a survey by the Institute of Governmental Studies (IGS) at the University of California, Berkeley recorded 48% support and 41% opposition.
Another poll, conducted by Politico and UC Berkeley’s Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research, put support this week at 45%, with 43% opposed and 12% undecided. However, among respondents who said they had heard “a lot” about the proposal, opposition reached 57% versus 38% in favor.
In 2022 Californians rejected Proposition 30, an initiative that would have raised taxes on higher earners. The result was 58% against and 42% in favor. The measure proposed raising the income tax by 1.75 percentage points on those earning more than $2 million a year and directing the new revenue to zero-emission vehicle programs and fire prevention.
In that context, the six Nobel Prize economists argue that, while Proposition 40 would not by itself solve the problem of inequality in California, it would represent a step in the right direction. “What will allow California to thrive in the future is not letting a handful of billionaires live tax free: it is adequate public spending on health, education, and public infrastructure, key engines of economic growth to which it is only fair to ask the ultra-wealthy to contribute,” they write.

>
This brief note reports the results of a survey of tax experts regarding California’s Proposition 40, a proposed one-time tax on billionaire wealth.
Among 105 respondents, 69.5 percent opposed the proposal, including 71.0 percent of economists and 85.0 percent of accountants.
Lawyers were more supportive, with 60.0 percent favoring the tax.
Open-ended responses reveal concerns about taxpayer mobility, revenue losses, valuation difficulties, and administrative costs.
The results contrast with the public endorsement of the proposal by six Nobel Prize-winning economists and highlight differences in opinion among scholars who specialize in taxation.
Opinions about Prop 40 embed knowledge of the relevant empirical literature, interpretation of the empirical literature, and the values of the person holding the opinion, such that differences between groups in opinion might reflect any of these factors.
> **Conclusion**
> Six Nobel Prize-winning economists have endorsed Proposition 40.
Among the respondents to this survey, however, economists and accountants who study taxes in their everyday work overwhelmingly oppose it, while lawyers are divided, marginally supporting it.
Overall, surveyed tax experts would not vote for Prop 40.

# About 70% of tax scholars would vote against California’s billionaire tax, a new survey finds
It turns out most academics who study taxes for a living would vote against California’s proposed billionaire tax, a new survey finds.
Jeff Hoopes, a professor at the University of North Carolina and research director of the UNC Tax Center, surveyed members of the National Tax Association, a professional group of mostly academic economists, accountants, and lawyers.
Of the 105 respondents, 73 (69.5%) said they would vote against Proposition 40, and 32 (30.5%) said they would vote for it.
Accountants were the most opposed, with 17 of 20 (85%) against the tax.
Among economists, 49 of 69 (71%) opposed the tax.
Meanwhile, among lawyers, nine of 15 (60%) favored the measure.
Law professors also wrote much of the new measure: Three of its principal drafters, Brian Galle, David Gamage, and Darien Shanske, are tax-law professors.
Overall, that comes out to seven out of 10 tax scholars who would think otherwise before voting on Prop 40—but it’s not because they oppose the idea behind it.
“The 70% of folks who would not vote for Prop 40 seems to have two different camps,” Hoopes told *Fortune*.
“Those who would favor wealth taxes in general, but just thought this particular version was bad, and those who don’t think a wealth tax is a good idea at all.”

What Do Tax Experts Think About California’s Billionaire Tax?
By
Jeff Hoopes (https://taxpolicynetwork.org/author/jeff-hoopes/)
October 14, 2026 October 14, 2026
Six Nobel Prize-winning economists (https://www.ft.com/content/94ec0fee-53ab-4d7e-9b17-6b05608ad974) recently endorsed California’s Proposition 40, a ballot initiative that would impose a one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth. Their Nobel-recognized contributions concern subjects such as labor markets, information, economic development, and other broad questions in economics, rather than the practical design and administration of taxes. While some of these scholars have studied taxes, none focused entirely on taxes. But it does raise a natural question. What do economists who specialize in taxation think about the proposal? And what do scholars in other disciplines, such as law and accounting, think? To find out, I surveyed researchers belonging to a prominent professional organization devoted to tax research and public finance. [1] Its membership draws heavily from academic economists, accountants, and lawyers. Their answers provide a different perspective on the debate.
Proposition 40 was developed largely by legal academics. Three of its principal drafters (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/facpubs/1351/), Brian Galle, David Gamage, and Darien Shanske, are tax-law professors. They worked with economist Emmanuel Saez of the University of California, Berkeley. Economist Gabriel Zucman has also been a prominent activist surrounding the measure and wealth taxation generally, publicly promoting wealth taxation and contributing with Saez and Jasper Boll to research estimating billionaire wealth and prospective revenues (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35218).
The measure (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) would impose a one-time tax of up to 5 percent on covered net wealth for individuals whose covered assets exceed $1 billion, generally using California residence as of January 1, 2026 (https://taxpolicynetwork.org/californias-proposed-billionaire-wealth-tax-and-the-question-of-state-residency/). Payment would be due in 2027 (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2026-news-releases-and-advisories/california-secretary-state-shirley-n-weber-phd-announces-new-measure-eligible-november-2026-general-election-ballot-imposes-one), with an option to pay over five years at additional cost. Covered property includes business interests and other financial and intangible assets, while real estate and certain retirement assets are generally excluded. Supporters estimate that the tax could generate approximately $100 billion in revenue. The amount ultimately collected depends on the size of the taxable base, valuation, compliance, litigation, and taxpayers’ responses.
Supporters argue that billionaire wealth has grown substantially and that taxing a portion of accumulated wealth would raise significant public revenue from taxpayers with considerable capacity to pay. They also see the proposal as a means of moderating economic inequality and the political influence associated with concentrated wealth. In the standard public-finance analysis, a genuinely unexpected, one-time tax on wealth already accumulated could create fewer distortions to past saving decisions than a tax that households anticipated when making those decisions. Supporters further argue that the retrospective residence date could limit the ability to avoid the levy by moving after the fact.
The objections concern both the revenue estimate (https://taxpolicynetwork.org/galle-v-rauh-comparing-two-revenue-estimates-for-california-billionaire-taxation/) and the operation of the tax. A state-level wealth tax may encourage wealthy residents to move, potentially eroding future income tax receipts even if a liability for the one-time levy has already accrued. Privately held businesses and other illiquid property are difficult to value and could generate costly disputes, liquidity problems, and avoidance opportunities. Other critics have raised concerns about accounting-based valuations (https://taxpolicynetwork.org/biases-inequities-and-adverse-incentives-from-basing-wealth-taxes-on-accounting-measures/), the difficulty of using one-time revenue for continuing expenditures (https://taxpolicynetwork.org/the-one-time-billionaire-tax-a-one-time-fix-for-a-permanent-problem/), and valuation and liquidity problems for closely held assets (https://taxpolicynetwork.org/californias-billionaire-tax-liquidity-issues-and-questionable-fiscal-rationale/).
One recent analysis (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6340778) suggests that the fiscal effect could even be negative. Joshua Rauh, Benjamin Jaros, Gregory Kearney, John Doran, and Matheus Cosso at Stanford’s Hoover Institution estimate that the levy would bring in substantially less than proponents project once departures and other reductions in the taxable base are considered. They further estimate that the present value of lost future state income tax revenues could exceed the wealth-tax collections. Their analysis finds a negative net fiscal effect under many plausible scenarios. These are model-based estimates that depend on assumptions about residence, litigation, taxpayer behavior, and discount rates, rather than observed outcomes of a tax that has not yet been imposed. Their estimates represent a substantial departure (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6428578) from the original, and substantially simpler, revenue estimates from proponents of the bill.
In order to see what scholars thought about the proposal, I surveyed researchers who specialize in taxation and public finance. The mailing list came from the directory of a prominent tax research organization. Its members include economists, accountants, lawyers, and other researchers, many of whom work at universities. I began with 503 contacts drawn from a somewhat dated directory (see footnote 1). Initial emails to these addresses generated 53 nondelivery notices. I located replacement email addresses for most of those failed emails, and ended up sending 486 apparently valid email addresses that did not bounce back. Note that the absence of a bounce does not guarantee that an email reached its intended recipient.
The questionnaire asked one substantive question. “If you had the chance, would you vote for Prop 40, imposing the tax?” Respondents chose either “Yes, I would vote for Prop 40 and impose the new tax” or “No, I would vote against Prop 40 and not impose the new tax.” As the organization whose membership directory I used has economists, lawyers, and accountants who study taxation, I also had survey participants identify as an economist, accountant, lawyer, or other respondent and could leave a comment. As of October 13, 2026, at 5.17 p.m. Eastern, I received 105 responses, equal to 21.6 percent of the cleaned invitation list. The poll was voluntary and completely anonymous. Because I did not collect identifying information or restrict responses to one per recipient, I cannot rule out that an individual answered more than once. Nor can I know whether respondents disproportionately held strong views. The results therefore describe the people who responded.
Of the 105 respondents, 73 (69.5 percent) would vote against Proposition 40 and 32 (30.5 percent) would vote in favor. Figure 1 reports the overall distribution. Approximately seven in ten respondents opposed the proposal.
The respondents identified primarily as economists (69, or 65.7 percent), accountants (20, or 19.0 percent), and lawyers (15, or 14.3 percent). One respondent selected other (and noted they were a political scientist, they are omitted from Figure 2). These groups differed markedly. Among economists, 49 of 69 (71.0 percent) opposed the tax. Among accountants, 17 of 20 (85.0 percent) opposed it. Among lawyers, nine of 15 (60.0 percent) favored the measure, while six (40.0 percent) opposed it. Figure 2 reports the distribution by profession. In the combined economics and accounting groups, 66 of 89 (74.2 percent) opposed Proposition 40.
Figure 2. Would you vote for Prop 40, separated by area of academic focus
Summary of Open-Ended Comments
I also left an optional field for comments, thoughts, or opinions about Proposition 40. Thirty-eight respondents used it, including 25 economists, six accountants, six lawyers, and one other respondent. The comments help explain why someone might oppose this proposal while supporting higher taxation of wealthy individuals. The AI generated summaries that follow paraphrase the responses rather than quote individual respondents.
Economists
Several opposed imposing a wealth tax at the state rather than federal level, citing migration, cross-border substitution, and the potential loss of future California income tax revenue.
Others objected to asset valuation, avoidance, and the administrative burdens of taxing privately held or illiquid wealth.
Multiple opponents said explicitly that they favored higher taxes on the wealthy, or would consider a federal wealth tax, but opposed this particular measure.
The one-time design drew objections about using temporary revenue for ongoing programs. one respondent preferred a lower-rate recurring levy instead.
Supporters emphasized the potential efficiency of a genuinely unexpected levy on wealth already accumulated, reducing concentrated wealth, and generating additional public revenue.
Accountants
Respondents emphasized practical implementation, including the challenge of administering a state-level levy and enforcing it across mobile taxpayers and assets.
Several pointed to valuation, liquidity, and compliance costs and questioned whether collections would justify those costs.
Some favored different methods of taxing wealthy households or opposed this proposal without opposing wealth taxation in principle.
Others raised objections to taxing wealth rather than realized income, including concerns about effective tax burdens, business certainty, and property rights.
Lawyers
Supporters stressed equity and the social and political consequences of widening wealth inequality.
Opponents worried that a nominally one-time tax could become a recurring levy with greater efficiency costs.
Some warned of businesses leaving California. others described the proposal as short-term fiscal policy.
One respondent selected opposition but described being on the fence, illustrating the limitations of a forced yes-or-no response.
The open-ended comments suggest that support for higher taxation of wealthy households and support for Proposition 40 are distinct questions. Some opponents objected to wealth taxation in general, but others objected to the state-level administration, one-time design, revenue implications, or choice of tax base. Conversely, some supporters acknowledged administrative or behavioral concerns but regarded the fiscal need or the distributional case as decisive.
Survey Integrity Checks
To protect respondents’ anonymity, I did not collect IP addresses or other identifying information. Consequently, it is possible that the same individual completed the survey more than once. To examine whether responses exhibited unusual clustering, I graphed the cumulative percentage voting against Proposition 40 in the order responses were received (Figure 3). The longest consecutive sequence of votes against the tax was 10 respondents. If responses were independent and randomly distributed with a 70 percent probability of voting against the tax, the probability of observing at least one sequence of 10 or more consecutive votes against the tax among 105 responses would be approximately 59.9 percent. The observed sequence is therefore not unusual under this model, although the exercise cannot rule out multiple responses from one individual.
Figure 3. Cumulative Opposition by Response Order
I also examined the elapsed time between consecutive responses (Figure 4). The median interval was 5.3 minutes, and the shortest was four seconds. Responses arrived rapidly after the initial invitation and became less frequent over subsequent days, with the longest interval reaching 40.7 hours. This pattern is consistent with a burst of replies after an email invitation and does not by itself establish that anyone submitted more than one response.
Figure 4. Time Between Consecutive Survey Responses
Conclusion
Six Nobel Prize-winning economists have endorsed Proposition 40. Among the respondents to this survey, however, economists and accountants who study taxes in their everyday work overwhelmingly oppose it, while lawyers are divided, marginally supporting it. Overall, surveyed tax experts would not vote for Prop 40.
Some of the relevant questions for assessing this piece of legislation are empirical. How many wealthy individuals will leave California? How much revenue will the tax actually raise? These are questions on which academic research can shed light. But whether the tax is desirable also depends on values, including how big government should be, who should pay for it, and how many economic resources we are willing to use up in the process of collecting revenue. Academic tax experts have expertise that can help answer the empirical questions, but their values are no more important than anyone else’s, even if they have likely thought about these tax issues more. However, in the end, considering both the empirical evidence they are aware of and their values, the tax scholars responding to this survey do not support Proposition 40 by a substantial margin.

Executive Summary
The Billionaire Tax Act (“BTA”) would assess a one-time 5% wealth tax on California billionaires, generating
an estimated $116 billion in revenue for the State of California, or $23.2 billion annually for five years.1 Over
this period, the expenditure of wealth tax revenues is estimated to support over 216,000 wage and salary
jobs in California annually—including nearly 150,000 direct jobs in the health care, food assistance, and
education sectors—and $45.7 billion in annual economic output. This activity would in turn generate, in
addition to the direct wealth tax revenue, an estimated $1.4 billion annually in personal income,
corporation and sales tax revenue for the state and local governments.
Available data suggest that the measure's filing has not affected California’s business climate (contrary to
claims made by the BTA’s opponents): across measures of early-stage investment, total venture capital
funding, and business formation, the state’s share of national activity has held steady or increased since
the measure’s introduction in October 2025. Moreover, even under aggressive assumptions regarding the
responsiveness of California’s billionaires to the BTA’s one-time wealth tax, revenue losses attributable to
the potential departures of some of the state’s billionaires are modest relative to the revenues raised by the
measure.
Estimation of Wealth Tax Revenue Generated by the BTA
The BTA would assess a one-time 5% tax on the total net worth, excluding directly held real estate, of
billionaires who were residents of California as of January 1, 2026 (i.e., the “tax obligation date”). For
purposes of calculating tax liability, the measure specifies that each billionaire’s taxable net worth will be
valued on December 31, 2026 (i.e., the “valuation date”).
The BTA is Expected to Generate $116.2 Billion of Wealth Tax Revenue
According to the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires List (the “Forbes List”), as of August 15, 2026, California was
home to 261 billionaires who together held a collective net worth of approximately $2.34 trillion.2 As a
result, after excluding the share of this wealth comprised of directly held real estate (an estimated 0.6% of
total net worth),3 the BTA’s one-time 5% wealth tax would generate an estimated $116.2 billion to fund BTA
initiatives. Because the BTA allows billionaire taxpayers to spread their tax liability over five equal annual
installments, it is expected that expenditures of wealth tax revenue will also be distributed over a five-year
period. Therefore, this report’s estimates of the BTA’s annual economic and fiscal impacts reflect an
estimated $23.2 billion of BTA expenditures annually (i.e., $116.2 billion divided by five years).

Sensitivity of Revenue Estimate to Billionaire Undercounting and Tax
Avoidance
Due to uncertainty regarding the potential underestimation of billionaire net worth, the undercounting of
billionaire residents of California, and billionaires’ avoidance of the tax through changes in residency, the
baseline estimate of the total billionaire net worth subject to the wealth tax (i.e., $2.34 trillion as of August
15, 2026) may understate or overstate the actual tax base.
Underestimates of net worth and undercounting of billionaires – The estimated number and wealth of
California’s billionaires used in this report are based on the Forbes List. While Forbes provides the only
publicly available data source identifying all taxpayers potentially subject to the BTA, a recent comparison
of Forbes’ and Bloomberg’s ranking of the 500 richest people notes that, due to differing methodologies for
estimating net worth, Bloomberg’s net worth estimates for California’s billionaires are, on average, 7.5%
higher than Forbes’ estimates.4
Separately, statistical analysis of the distribution of Forbes List billionaires by Boll et al. (2026) suggests
that the list excludes many billionaires with net worths of less than $5 billion. If the estimated combined net
worth of these “missing” billionaires is included in the BTA’s estimated tax base, wealth tax revenue would
increase by $24.6 billion (or 21.2% of the baseline).5
Together, these two adjustments to Forbes’ net worth estimates would combine to generate a 30.2%
increase in the wealth tax base above the baseline estimate.6
Wealth tax avoidance – Because the wealth tax is imposed only on individuals who were California
residents as of the measure’s January 1, 2026, tax obligation date, the BTA could raise less than $116 billion
if some of the state’s billionaires established nonresidency, for state tax law purposes, prior to this date.
Since the measure’s filing in October 2025, news reports have identified five California billionaires who took
steps to relocate to other states prior to January 1, 2026; these individuals account for roughly $588 billion
of the $2.34 trillion of total California billionaire net worth, or approximately $29.2 billion of future wealth
tax revenue.7 Additionally, some observers have noted that the wealth tax could be deemed a “retroactive”
tax prohibited by the United States Constitution. If such a challenge were successful, a court could
effectively shift the tax obligation date to Election Day, resulting in a further reduction of wealth tax

Economic and Fiscal Impacts of BTA Expenditures
The state’s expenditures of wealth tax revenue on health care, food assistance, and education programs
would generate a net increase in economic activity and employment statewide.
BTA Economic Impact Estimates

consumption, the wealth tax would draw almost entirely on funds that would not otherwise have entered
the California economy. As a result, the net increase in spending on goods and services under the BTA is
approximately equal to the amount of wealth tax revenue raised each year.13

Endorsement: California isn’t a lab rat. Prop 40 treats us like one
There’s no denying the visceral satisfaction of a billionaire bloodletting. But will the measure’s wealth tax actually help the state?
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:42 p.m.
Taxation, like everything else in life, is an exercise in trade-offs.
How much public good can a tax extract before it passes the tipping point into harm?
As it relates to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php) on California’s November ballot, many believe you don’t have to look very hard to find where the cost-benefit needle falls.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on anyone whose total net worth is greater than $1 billion as of Dec. 31, 2026, and who was a California resident on Jan. 1, 2026. After administrative costs, 90% of the revenue would go to public healthcare, while the other 10% would go to food assistance and education. The total collected could range from $28 billion to $100 billion — depending on whose math you believe. (California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the state will “probably” (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) collect “tens of billions.”)

Whatever the total, there’s no denying that California billionaires — who by some counts control a combined $2 trillion (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) in wealth — can afford to shoulder it.
Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and a coauthor of Prop 40, called the measure a “rounding error” on the fortunes of California’s wealthiest.
For this mostly bloodless toll, Californians get relief from President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful” Medicaid cuts and radiate with satisfaction at sending a landmark message about wealth inequality.
Or so it would seem.

Is Prop 40 so flawlessly executed that California has nothing to lose if it passes?
Opposition from the California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood, California Medical Association, the NAACP, California Professional Firefighters and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California suggests not.
Let’s start with the healthcare organizations, which would effectively receive 90% of Prop 40’s funds. Why are they opposed?
Dustin Corcoran, CEO of the California Medical Association, said in an endorsement interview that there’s no guarantee Prop 40’s payload will arrive in time to backfill Trump’s cuts. The state has no existing system for assessing billionaire wealth, he said, and it will likely take years to develop one.
Corcoran cited his experience as a backer of Prop 56, which passed in 2016 and imposed a tax on vape products.

“It probably took the Franchise Tax Board 10 years of us beating them up because they couldn’t figure out how to get the tax right,” he said. “And that was a fairly straightforward thing to try and figure out.”
Even if the money does land, and that’s a big if, Corcoran argued that weak “anti-supplantation” protections in the measure will allow lawmakers to spend its revenue however they see fit — undermining one of Prop 40’s most powerful arguments, the urgency of the moment for healthcare.
University of Missouri School of Law Professor David Gamage, one of Prop 40’s coauthors, disputed these notions. He estimated that “75% of billionaire wealth is in publicly traded assets,” making much of it easy to track. And even if the measure does have supplantation holes, political pressure will prevent California politicians from treating Prop 40 revenue like a slush fund.
These vague assurances don’t persuade Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California. Healthcare organizations like hers, she said, use forward-looking budgets. They can’t commit to providing services if they can’t definitively rely on money coming in to pay for them.
Meanwhile, Prop 40 puts the money Hicks can count on in jeopardy.

That’s because California’s budget is overly dependent on income taxes — roughly half of which (https://lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/7)historically come from the ultra-wealthy top 1% of taxpayers.
Studying the impacts of Prop 40 “was an eye-opening experience for what California’s tax structure is and how the wealthy are a part of it,” Hicks said.
This gets at the real questions surrounding Prop 40 and why so many otherwise progressive organizations oppose the tax: Will billionaires leave the state if the measure passes, and will they take their companies with them?
“Good riddance” is the popular retort among online commentators.
But that attitude is childish and self-defeating. A recent case study explained why.
